revision_notes.title: Discrete Mathematics: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Discrete Mathematics questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: In every finite undirected graph, the sum of vertex degrees is twice the number of edges.
An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
A tree with n vertices has n - 1 edges.
common_traps: Do not assume that every partial order is a total order.
Do not assume that every group is commutative.
Do not assume that a simple cycle on n vertices has n - 1 edges.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A simple complete graph has 6 vertices. How many edges does it contain? Reasoning: Every unordered vertex pair is an edge, so C(6, 2) = 6*5/2 = 15.

revision_notes.title: Linear Algebra: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Linear Algebra questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: The determinant equals the product of eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity.
A square system with a nonsingular coefficient matrix has a unique solution.
Every real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues.
common_traps: Do not assume that every square matrix is diagonalizable.
Do not assume that a zero determinant implies a unique solution for every right-hand side.
Do not assume that row operations never change a determinant.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: An upper triangular 3 x 3 matrix has diagonal entries 3, 4, and 5. Find its determinant. Reasoning: The determinant of a triangular matrix is the diagonal product: 3*4*5 = 60.

revision_notes.title: Calculus: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Calculus questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Differentiability at a point implies continuity there.
An interior differentiable local extremum must have zero derivative.
The fundamental theorem links definite integration and antiderivatives.
common_traps: Do not assume that continuity at a point always implies differentiability there.
Do not assume that every stationary point is a local maximum.
Do not assume that a differentiable function can have a jump discontinuity.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: For f(x) = 2x^2 + 3x + 3, find f'(2). Reasoning: f'(x) = 4x + 3; substituting x=2 gives 11.

revision_notes.title: Probability and Statistics: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Probability and Statistics questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: For a binomial random variable, the mean is np.
Independent events A and B satisfy P(A intersection B) = P(A)P(B).
Variance is unchanged when a constant is added to a random variable.
common_traps: Do not assume that mutually exclusive nonempty events are independent.
Do not assume that for every random variable, variance equals its mean.
Do not assume that conditional probabilities P(A given B) and P(B given A) are always equal.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: X is binomial with n=9 and p=3/10. Find E[X]. Reasoning: For a binomial variable E[X]=np=9*3/10=2.7.

revision_notes.title: Boolean Algebra: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Boolean Algebra questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: De Morgan's law gives complement(AB) = complement(A) + complement(B).
A canonical minterm contains every variable exactly once.
X XOR X is always zero.
common_traps: Do not assume that x + XY equals X + Y.
Do not assume that a maxterm evaluates to zero for every input assignment.
Do not assume that x AND complement(X) equals one.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A Boolean function of 5 variables is 1 exactly when 2 inputs are 1. How many minterms make it 1? Reasoning: Choose the 2 asserted variables: C(5, 2) = 10.

revision_notes.title: Combinational Circuits: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Combinational Circuits questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: A combinational circuit has no state memory.
A decoder with n inputs can have up to 2^n output lines.
A full adder accepts three one-bit inputs.
common_traps: Do not assume that a multiplexer with s select lines has only s data inputs.
Do not assume that a half adder has a carry-in input.
Do not assume that a combinational output depends on the previous clock cycle.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: How many data inputs does a multiplexer with 3 select lines require? Reasoning: Each select word chooses one input, so the count is 2^3 = 8.

revision_notes.title: Sequential Circuits: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Sequential Circuits questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: A sequential circuit can depend on stored state.
A D flip-flop samples its input at its active clock event.
A modulo-m counter needs at least ceil(log2(m)) state bits.
common_traps: Do not assume that every latch is edge triggered.
Do not assume that a sequential circuit has no feedback path.
Do not assume that a k-bit binary counter has only k distinct states.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: What is the minimum number of flip-flops for a counter with 8 distinct states? Reasoning: Choose the least k with 2^k >= 8; k = ceil(log2(8)) = 3.

revision_notes.title: Number Representation and Arithmetic: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Number Representation and Arithmetic questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: An n-bit unsigned word has 2^n distinct patterns.
The n-bit two's-complement range is -2^(n-1) through 2^(n-1)-1.
Two's-complement negation complements the bits and adds one.
common_traps: Do not assume that an n-bit unsigned word has maximum value 2^n.
Do not assume that sign extension changes the represented two's-complement value.
Do not assume that adding two positive two's-complement values can never overflow.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: How many distinct values can a 5-bit unsigned word represent? Reasoning: There are two choices per bit, giving 2^5 = 32 patterns.

revision_notes.title: Machine Instructions and Addressing Modes: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Machine Instructions and Addressing Modes questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Immediate addressing places the operand value in the instruction.
Base-plus-offset addressing adds a displacement to a base register.
Indirect addressing requires an additional memory reference for the effective address.
common_traps: Do not assume that immediate addressing always fetches the operand from data memory.
Do not assume that register addressing names a memory location only.
Do not assume that pC-relative addressing cannot support branches.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A base register contains address 1064; an instruction uses displacement 16. Find the base-plus-offset effective address. Reasoning: Effective address = base + displacement = 1064 + 16 = 1080.

revision_notes.title: ALU, Datapath and Control: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: ALU, Datapath and Control questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: The ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations.
A datapath contains storage and functional units connected by buses.
A control unit selects datapath operations for each instruction.
common_traps: Do not assume that the program counter is part of secondary storage.
Do not assume that a hardwired control unit stores every control word in a writable cache.
Do not assume that an ALU alone determines the instruction sequence.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: An ALU first adds 18 and 4, then logically shifts the result left by 2 bit(s). Find the unsigned result. Reasoning: The sum is 22; left shifting by 2 multiplies by 2^2, giving 88.

revision_notes.title: Instruction Pipelining: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Instruction Pipelining questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Ideal pipelining improves throughput, not the latency of one instruction.
A load-use dependency can require a stall even with forwarding.
A branch can create a control hazard.
common_traps: Do not assume that forwarding removes every possible pipeline stall.
Do not assume that a structural hazard is caused only by branch instructions.
Do not assume that an ideal k-stage pipeline completes n instructions in kn cycles.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A 5-stage pipeline executes 9 instructions and incurs 1 total stall cycle(s). How many cycles are required? Reasoning: Ideal cycles are 5+9-1; adding 1 stalls gives 14.

revision_notes.title: Memory Hierarchy: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Memory Hierarchy questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Temporal locality means recently used data is likely to be reused.
Average memory access time includes hit time plus miss rate times miss penalty.
A larger block can exploit spatial locality.
common_traps: Do not assume that a cache miss never accesses a lower memory level.
Do not assume that direct-mapped caches have no conflict misses.
Do not assume that write-through updates only the cache copy.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A cache hit takes 2 ns, miss rate is 10%, and additional miss penalty is 25 ns. Find AMAT in ns. Reasoning: AMAT = 2 + (10/100)*25 = 4.5 ns.

revision_notes.title: I/O Interface: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: I/O Interface questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Programmed I/O can make the CPU poll device status.
Interrupt-driven I/O lets a device notify the processor.
Memory-mapped I/O uses ordinary address-space operations.
common_traps: Do not assume that interrupt-driven I/O requires continuous polling.
Do not assume that programmed I/O always transfers blocks without CPU involvement.
Do not assume that every I/O device executes CPU instructions directly.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A programmed-I/O loop performs 25 status polls, each costing 4 CPU cycles. Find total polling cycles. Reasoning: Total polling cost is 25*4 = 100 cycles.

revision_notes.title: Interrupts and DMA: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Interrupts and DMA questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: DMA can transfer a block with limited CPU intervention.
A vectored interrupt identifies an interrupt-service entry.
Cycle stealing lets DMA use individual memory-bus cycles.
common_traps: Do not assume that dMA requires one CPU instruction for every transferred byte.
Do not assume that interrupt masking physically disconnects all devices.
Do not assume that a non-vectored interrupt always supplies the ISR address directly.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A DMA controller transfers 40 words and occupies the bus for 3 cycles per word. Find occupied bus cycles. Reasoning: The transfer occupies 40*3 = 120 bus cycles.

revision_notes.title: Programming in C: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Programming in C questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the pointed-to type size.
Array indexing a[i] is defined using pointer arithmetic.
C passes ordinary function arguments by value.
common_traps: Do not assume that incrementing an int pointer always adds one byte.
Do not assume that a local automatic variable persists after its function returns.
Do not assume that c arrays perform bounds checks automatically.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: In C, an array starts at byte address 1128; each element is 2 byte(s). Find the address of element a[3]. Reasoning: Row address arithmetic gives 1128+3*2 = 1134.

revision_notes.title: Recursion: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Recursion questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: A terminating recursion needs progress toward a base case.
Each active recursive call has its own activation record.
A recursive algorithm can be described by a recurrence.
common_traps: Do not assume that every recursive function uses constant stack space.
Do not assume that a base case makes the first call unnecessary.
Do not assume that tail recursion always has exponential running time.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A function F(k) makes exactly one call to F(k-1) for k>0 and stops at F(0). Including the base call, how many calls arise from F(5)? Reasoning: The calls are F(5), F(4), ..., F(0): 5+1 = 6.

revision_notes.title: Arrays: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Arrays questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Array elements occupy contiguous storage.
C stores multidimensional arrays in row-major order.
Random access by index is constant time for an array.
common_traps: Do not assume that inserting at the front of a dense array is always constant time.
Do not assume that an array index can never be computed arithmetically.
Do not assume that column-major order is mandated by C.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A row-major int A[5][6] starts at address 2000 with 4-byte elements. Find address A[1][2]. Reasoning: Linear index = 1*6+2=8; address = 2000+4*8=2032.

revision_notes.title: Stacks and Queues: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Stacks and Queues questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: A stack uses last-in, first-out order.
A queue uses first-in, first-out order.
A circular queue reuses positions released at the front.
common_traps: Do not assume that a queue removes the newest element first.
Do not assume that a stack requires sorted keys.
Do not assume that a circular queue cannot be implemented with an array.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: An array circular queue has 9 slots and uses one empty slot to distinguish full from empty. What is its usable capacity? Reasoning: One slot is reserved, so usable capacity is 9-1=8.

revision_notes.title: Linked Lists: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Linked Lists questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: A singly linked node stores a link to its successor.
Insertion after a known node can be constant time.
A doubly linked list supports traversal in both directions.
common_traps: Do not assume that a linked list provides constant-time access to its kth node without extra indexing.
Do not assume that every linked-list node is contiguous with the next node.
Do not assume that deleting a node never changes any link.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: Traversing a singly linked list of 12 nodes follows 11 next links, each costing 3 time units. Find total link-following cost. Reasoning: There are 12-1 links, so cost = 11*3=33.

revision_notes.title: Trees and Binary Search Trees: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Trees and Binary Search Trees questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Inorder traversal of a BST visits distinct keys in sorted order.
A tree with n vertices has n - 1 edges.
A binary tree node has at most two children.
common_traps: Do not assume that preorder traversal of every BST is sorted.
Do not assume that every binary tree is height balanced.
Do not assume that a complete binary tree must have an odd number of nodes.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A perfect binary tree has root at height 0 and overall height 3. How many nodes does it have? Reasoning: Nodes = 1+2+...+2^3 = 2^4-1 = 15.

revision_notes.title: Heaps: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Heaps questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: A binary heap is a complete binary tree.
The maximum key is at the root of a max-heap.
Insertion can require a path of swaps toward the root.
common_traps: Do not assume that a max-heap stores all keys in sorted array order.
Do not assume that searching an arbitrary key in a binary heap is always logarithmic.
Do not assume that the root of a min-heap contains the maximum key.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: In a 1-indexed binary heap, what is the parent index of the node at index 11? Reasoning: For a 1-indexed heap, parent(i)=floor(i/2), so floor(11/2)=5.

revision_notes.title: Graphs: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Graphs questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: An adjacency list uses O(V + E) space for a sparse graph.
An undirected edge appears twice in ordinary adjacency lists.
An adjacency matrix supports constant-time edge lookup.
common_traps: Do not assume that every graph is connected.
Do not assume that an adjacency matrix uses O(V + E) space in all cases.
Do not assume that a directed edge must appear twice in an adjacency list.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: An undirected simple graph has 10 edges. How many neighbor entries occur across all ordinary adjacency lists? Reasoning: Each edge is listed at both endpoints, giving 2*10=20 entries.

revision_notes.title: Searching, Sorting and Hashing: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Searching, Sorting and Hashing questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Binary search requires an ordered search interval.
Comparison sorting has an Omega(n log n) worst-case lower bound in the general model.
A hash collision occurs when distinct keys map to one slot.
common_traps: Do not assume that binary search is correct on an arbitrary unsorted array.
Do not assume that every hash table operation is worst-case O(1).
Do not assume that merge sort is an in-place constant-space algorithm in its standard array implementation.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A binary-search candidate interval has 32 items. How many exact halvings reduce it to one item? Reasoning: 32=2^5; therefore 5 halvings leave one candidate.

revision_notes.title: Complexity Analysis: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Complexity Analysis questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Theta notation gives an asymptotically tight bound.
Constants are ignored in asymptotic growth classes.
A polynomial-time bound is closed under addition and multiplication.
common_traps: Do not assume that o(n) and Omega(n) are mutually exclusive.
Do not assume that every exponential algorithm is faster than every polynomial algorithm for all inputs.
Do not assume that worst-case time can be smaller than best-case time.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A nested loop executes its inner statement i times for i=1 through 6. How many total executions occur? Reasoning: The count is 1+...+6=6*7/2=21.

revision_notes.title: Divide and Conquer: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Divide and Conquer questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Divide and conquer solves subproblems and combines their results.
Merge sort has logarithmically many merge levels.
Binary search discards about half the remaining interval.
common_traps: Do not assume that every divide-and-conquer recurrence has quadratic complexity.
Do not assume that merge sort performs no combine work.
Do not assume that divide and conquer cannot be implemented recursively.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: Merge sort is run on 16 items. How many halving levels occur before singleton subarrays? Reasoning: Because 16=2^4, log2(16)=4 halving levels occur.

revision_notes.title: Greedy Algorithms: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Greedy Algorithms questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Kruskal's algorithm adds safe edges in nondecreasing weight order.
Prim's algorithm grows one tree.
A greedy proof commonly uses an exchange argument.
common_traps: Do not assume that a locally best choice is optimal for every optimization problem.
Do not assume that kruskal's algorithm may retain a cycle in an MST.
Do not assume that every shortest-path problem permits negative cycles.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A connected graph has 6 vertices. How many edges are in any spanning tree? Reasoning: Every tree on 6 vertices contains 6-1=5 edges.

revision_notes.title: Dynamic Programming: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Dynamic Programming questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Dynamic programming exploits overlapping subproblems.
Memoization is top-down caching.
Tabulation stores subproblem answers in an evaluation order.
common_traps: Do not assume that dynamic programming never uses extra memory.
Do not assume that optimal substructure is irrelevant to dynamic programming.
Do not assume that memoization recomputes every subproblem each time.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: An LCS table includes row/column zero for strings of lengths 4 and 6. How many DP cells are stored? Reasoning: The table dimensions are (4+1) by (6+1), giving 35 cells.

revision_notes.title: Graph Algorithms: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Graph Algorithms questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: BFS finds shortest unweighted path lengths from a source.
DFS can identify connected components.
Dijkstra's standard correctness requires nonnegative edge weights.
common_traps: Do not assume that bFS always finds minimum-weight paths with arbitrary edge weights.
Do not assume that dFS uses a FIFO queue as its defining discipline.
Do not assume that dijkstra's algorithm remains correct with a reachable negative cycle.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: BFS scans adjacency lists of an undirected graph with 12 edges. How many edge entries are examined in total? Reasoning: Each undirected edge occurs in two adjacency lists, so 24 entries are scanned.

revision_notes.title: Regular Expressions and Finite Automata: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Regular Expressions and Finite Automata questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Regular expressions and finite automata define the same language class.
Every DFA is also an NFA.
Subset construction can produce up to 2^n DFA states from n NFA states.
common_traps: Do not assume that a finite automaton recognizes every context-free language.
Do not assume that an NFA is more expressive than a DFA.
Do not assume that a DFA may have two transitions on one symbol from the same state.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: Subset construction is applied to an NFA with 4 states. What is the maximum number of DFA subset states? Reasoning: There are 2^4 subsets, hence at most 16 DFA states.

revision_notes.title: Context-Free Grammars: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Context-Free Grammars questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: A context-free production has one nonterminal on its left side.
A parse tree records a grammatical derivation.
An ambiguous grammar has a string with two distinct parse trees.
common_traps: Do not assume that every context-free grammar is unambiguous.
Do not assume that a regular language cannot have a context-free grammar.
Do not assume that a leftmost derivation expands the rightmost nonterminal first.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A full binary parse tree has 4 terminal leaves. How many total nodes does it contain? Reasoning: A full binary tree with L leaves has L-1 internal nodes, so total = 2L-1 = 7.

revision_notes.title: Pushdown Automata: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Pushdown Automata questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: A pushdown automaton has an unbounded stack.
Nondeterministic PDAs recognize the context-free languages.
A stack can match nested delimiters.
common_traps: Do not assume that a PDA has only finite memory in total.
Do not assume that every Turing-recognizable language is accepted by a PDA.
Do not assume that a PDA stack supports random access to every stored symbol.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A PDA for a^k b^k pushes one marker per a. What is its maximum marker count on input a^5b^5? Reasoning: It pushes once for each of the 5 leading a symbols, reaching 5 markers.

revision_notes.title: Pumping Lemmas and Language Properties: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Pumping Lemmas and Language Properties questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: The regular languages are closed under complement.
A pumping lemma can be used to prove that a language is not regular.
Context-free languages are closed under union.
common_traps: Do not assume that the regular pumping lemma proves that a language is regular.
Do not assume that context-free languages are closed under intersection.
Do not assume that every subset of a regular language is regular.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A regular-language pumping lemma supplies pumping length p=6. What is the minimum string length to which its decomposition guarantee applies? Reasoning: The guarantee applies to every string whose length is at least p, so the minimum is 6.

revision_notes.title: Turing Machines and Undecidability: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Turing Machines and Undecidability questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: A Turing machine has a finite control and an unbounded tape model.
The halting problem is undecidable.
A mapping reduction can transfer undecidability to a target problem.
common_traps: Do not assume that every recognizable language is decidable.
Do not assume that a Turing machine tape has a fixed finite bound independent of input.
Do not assume that an undecidable language has no recognizer.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A Turing-machine head initially scans the leftmost symbol of a 6-symbol unary input. It moves right once per step. How many head moves are required before it first scans the blank immediately to the right of the input? Reasoning: Starting on the first input symbol, move 5 times to reach the last symbol and once more to reach the blank: 5+1=6.

revision_notes.title: Lexical Analysis: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Lexical Analysis questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: A lexer groups characters into tokens.
Regular expressions commonly specify token patterns.
Whitespace can often be discarded by lexical analysis.
common_traps: Do not assume that a lexer builds the complete parse tree.
Do not assume that context-free parsing is required to recognize every identifier.
Do not assume that a lexeme is always a token category rather than source text.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A source fragment contains 3 identifier lexemes, 2 operator lexemes, and 3 numeric literals, with whitespace ignored. How many tokens are emitted? Reasoning: Each listed lexeme yields one token: 3+2+3=8.

revision_notes.title: Parsing: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Parsing questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: LL parsing is top down.
LR parsing is bottom up.
FIRST and FOLLOW sets help construct predictive parsing tables.
common_traps: Do not assume that shift-reduce parsing is top down.
Do not assume that an LL(1) parser uses unlimited lookahead.
Do not assume that every context-free grammar is LR(0).
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: A simple shift-reduce trace shifts 6 tokens and performs 5 reductions. How many shift/reduce actions occur? Reasoning: Actions = 6 shifts + 5 reductions = 11.

revision_notes.title: Syntax-Directed Translation: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Syntax-Directed Translation questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Synthesized attributes are computed from child information.
Inherited attributes can pass context from parent or siblings.
A syntax-directed definition associates attributes and rules with grammar symbols or productions.
common_traps: Do not assume that every attribute must be inherited.
Do not assume that attribute evaluation never depends on a parse tree.
Do not assume that a synthesized attribute can only be supplied by the lexer.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: An attributed full binary expression tree has 4 leaves and one synthesized-value evaluation at every node. How many evaluations occur? Reasoning: The tree has 4+(4-1)=7 nodes, hence 7 evaluations.

revision_notes.title: Runtime Environments: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Runtime Environments questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: An activation record can store a return address.
Recursive calls require distinct active records.
Static links can support access to lexically enclosing scopes.
common_traps: Do not assume that all recursive calls share one set of local variables.
Do not assume that a return address is stored only in source code.
Do not assume that stack allocation can never support procedure calls.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: At maximum recursion depth 4, every activation record occupies 24 bytes. Find active-record storage in bytes. Reasoning: Storage = depth*record size = 4*24=96 bytes.

revision_notes.title: Intermediate Code Generation: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Intermediate Code Generation questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: Three-address code limits the number of explicit operands per instruction.
Temporaries can name intermediate expression results.
An abstract syntax tree omits some concrete grammar detail.
common_traps: Do not assume that three-address code requires exactly three machine registers.
Do not assume that intermediate code is always target-machine binary.
Do not assume that a temporary can never be reused.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: An expression tree has 4 binary operator nodes. With one three-address instruction per operator, how many instructions are emitted? Reasoning: Each operator produces one instruction, giving 4 instructions.

revision_notes.title: Code Optimization and Data-Flow Analysis: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: Code Optimization and Data-Flow Analysis questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: A live variable may be used along a future path before redefinition.
Common-subexpression elimination can avoid repeated computation.
Constant propagation substitutes known constant values.
common_traps: Do not assume that dead-code elimination must preserve every unreachable assignment.
Do not assume that liveness is a forward-only property by definition.
Do not assume that optimization may change the observable program result.
revision_notes.reasoning_pattern: Model question: The same available expression is computed 3 times without operand redefinition. How many computations can common-subexpression elimination remove? Reasoning: Keep the first computation and replace the remaining 3-1=2.

revision_notes.title: System Calls: GATE revision notes
revision_notes.summary: System Calls questions depend on its defining properties and a careful application of the standard calculation pattern.
key_points: A system call transfers control to a privileged kernel routine.
A read system call can block while waiting for I/O.
User programs request protected services through the system-call interface.
common_traps: Do not assume that a system call executes entirely without entering kernel mode.
Do not assume that every library call is necessarily a system call.
